summary: Shares observations on implementations of POP3, the Post Office Protocol. It is informational and does not define a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Notes from people who built mail pickup programs, saying what they learned so others can do better.

questions: what issues arise in pop3 implementations
subtitle: Real-world variations in how mail servers and clients handle POP3.

tldr.problem: POP3 implementations diverged from the standard in ways that created compatibility issues, and popular clients depended on optional features.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents observed implementation differences, particularly how some mail clients expect a space after the status indicator even though the RFC does not require it, and how clients depend on optional commands like UIDL and TOP.
tldr.outcome: Serves as guidance for implementers to maintain backward compatibility with widely-used but non-compliant software.

today: This memo updates RFC 1939 by documenting implementation variations. It remains relevant as a reference for implementers encountering legacy POP3 software.

sections.title: Implementation Variations
sections.content:
RFC 1957 documents observations on POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) implementations that diverge from the standard. Sometimes an implementation becomes so widely used that it becomes a de facto standard, even when it does not comply with the published specification.

This memo serves as practical guidance for implementers who must maintain compatibility with popular but non-compliant software.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC notes that some mail programs do things differently from the official rules, and other programs have learned to expect those differences.

sections.title: Status Indicator Format
sections.content:
The widely-used UCB POP3 server implementation, popper, always places a space following the status indicator in responses. Although the POP3 standard does not require this space, two popular mail clients—the Unix utility popclient and the proprietary netApp Systems Internet Series—expect it and fail without it.

The memo documents this mismatch so that implementers are aware of the requirement for backward compatibility, even though the RFC does not mandate it. Authors of both clients were contacted, and newer versions were released to handle both formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Some popular mail client programs expect an extra space in the server's response, even though the rules do not require it. New versions were fixed, but old ones still need that space.

sections.title: Optional Features in Wide Use
sections.content:
The POP3 specification defines several features as optional, but popular clients have created de facto requirements. Netscape requires the UIDL (Unique Identifier Listing) command, while Eudora requires TOP (read message header without fetching the full message).

The APOP (Authenticated Post Office Protocol) command provides better security than the standard login method, but adoption remained low as of 1996. Newer versions of the Qualcomm POP server and clients like GNU Emacs VM and Eudora added APOP support.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail programs depend on optional features even though they are not required. As time went on, more servers and clients added support for the safer APOP login method.

references.text: Myers, J., and M. Rose, "Post Office Protocol - Version 3", STD 53, RFC 1939, May 1996.
